data.source_title: Effect of Medication Reconciliation at Hospital Admission on 30-Day Returns to Hospital: A Randomized Clinical Trial
data.locator: Intervention; admission BPMH, pharmacist comparison, discrepancy communication and order adaptation
data.source_setting: Two regional secondary teaching hospitals in southern Switzerland; inpatient wards
value: Pharmacy assistant obtains a best possible medication history
Clinical pharmacist compares it with the physician-recorded home-medication list
Discrepancies are communicated to the attending physician and admission orders may be adapted
data.source_evidence_basis: The trial describes reconciliation as gathering a comprehensive current-medication history, comparing it with the admission list, then communicating discrepancies for clinician review and any needed order changes.
data.limitations: The intervention was studied in two Swiss hospitals and a selected high-risk population; staffing roles and procedures may differ elsewhere. This is a workflow reference, not RWJ policy.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Represent medication history capture, source comparison, discrepancy review, and clinician resolution as linked tasks with ownership and timestamps. Keep home medication history distinct from inpatient prescribing; do not encode drug or dose advice.

data.source_title: Effect of Medication Reconciliation at Hospital Admission on 30-Day Returns to Hospital: A Randomized Clinical Trial
data.locator: Results; discrepancies identified in intervention group during admission reconciliation
data.source_setting: Two regional secondary teaching hospitals in southern Switzerland; patients aged at least 85 years and/or with more than 10 admission medications
data.source_n: 866 intervention participants; 830 had at least one discrepancy
data.quantity: Intervention participants with at least one medication discrepancy
data.source_evidence_basis: Among 866 intervention participants, 830 (96.0%) had one or more discrepancies, with median 6 per patient (IQR 4–9). Omission was the most frequent discrepancy category reported.
data.limitations: Selected older and/or polypharmacy cohort; findings are not a general inpatient prevalence estimate. Detection is specific to the intervention and local medication-history process.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Use only as evidence that reconciliation may expose a substantial discrepancy workload in a selected cohort. If illustrating queues, label the cohort and keep counts distinct from local incidence; do not generate patient-specific medication content.

data.source_title: Effect of Medication Reconciliation at Hospital Admission on 30-Day Returns to Hospital: A Randomized Clinical Trial
data.locator: Primary outcome; unplanned all-cause hospital returns within 30 days after discharge
data.source_setting: Two regional secondary teaching hospitals in southern Switzerland; selected older/polypharmacy inpatient population
data.source_period: November 1, 2018 to January 15, 2020; outcome followed 30 days after discharge
data.quantity: Participants with composite unplanned hospital return within 30 days
data.source_evidence_basis: The randomized trial found 30-day unplanned visits or readmissions in 39.3% of intervention participants and 39.5% of controls (P=.93); the measured patient-centered endpoint did not differ.
data.limitations: This selected population and intervention do not establish that reconciliation is ineffective for other outcomes or settings. Do not interpret a null return outcome as evidence that discrepancies are harmless.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Separate process measures (history collected, discrepancies found/resolved) from downstream outcomes; do not assume a specific reduction in length of stay, readmission, or adverse events from completing a reconciliation task.
